questions.text: Based on the specifications in "Law QA Deck RA 7277 9442 10754", if a project requires 6 m, what is the correct interpretation?

options.text: 6 m is the minimum/standard requirement
6 m is the maximum permitted value
6 m applies only to specific conditions
6 m is an approximate value subject to interpretation

questions.rationale: The article specifies 6 m as the requirement. Context: from **₱50,000 up to around ₱300,000**, with imprisonment periods from about **6...

questions.text: Under RA 7277 and its implementing regulations, what additional income tax deduction can an employer claim for wages paid to qualified PWD employees?

options.text: An additional 10% of total PWD wages, deductible from gross income on top of the regular salary deduction, providing a modest incentive for hiring PWDs
An additional 25% of total salaries paid to qualified PWD employees, deductible from gross income on top of the regular salary expense
An additional 50% of total PWD wages, but only for employers with more than 500 employees, encouraging larger companies to hire PWDs
A flat ₱50,000 annual tax credit per qualified PWD employee regardless of actual wages paid, simplifying the tax filing process

rationale.summary: Employers can claim an additional 25% deduction on total salaries paid to qualified PWD employees, on top of the regular salary deduction.
rationale.explanation: RA 7277 and its BIR implementing regulations (e.g., RR 8-93) provide that employers may deduct an additional 25% of total salaries/wages paid to qualified PWD employees from their gross income — on top of the standard 100% salary deduction they already claim. This incentivizes private employment of PWDs. The deduction is subject to revenue regulations and must be properly documented.
common_misconceptions: Confusing the 25% wage deduction with the 50% deduction for accessibility improvements
Believing the incentive is a tax credit rather than a deduction

questions.explanation: This question tests the 25% additional wage deduction for PWD employees — frequently confused with the 50% accessibility improvement deduction, which is a different incentive.

questions.text: Which law explicitly criminalizes the public ridicule and vilification of PWDs, and what type of provision does it insert into RA 7277?

options.text: RA 10754 — it inserts a tax penalty clause for businesses that ridicule PWD customers
RA 9442 — it inserts specific penal provisions on public ridicule and vilification into RA 7277
BP 344 — it adds anti-ridicule provisions as part of the 2024 IRR update to the Accessibility Law
RA 7277 itself — the original Magna Carta already contained anti-ridicule criminal penalties at enactment

rationale.summary: RA 9442 (2007) inserts specific penal provisions on public ridicule and vilification into RA 7277.
rationale.explanation: RA 9442, enacted in 2007 as an amendment to RA 7277, adds explicit penal provisions criminalizing public ridicule and vilification of PWDs. These provisions recognize that discrimination against PWDs extends beyond physical access barriers to include social humiliation and degrading treatment. RA 10754 (2016) focuses on financial benefits (VAT exemption, expanded discounts) and does not add anti-ridicule provisions.
common_misconceptions: Attributing anti-ridicule provisions to RA 10754, which deals primarily with financial benefits
Believing anti-ridicule provisions were in RA 7277 from 1992

questions.explanation: This question tests which law added the anti-ridicule criminal provisions — a distinction between RA 9442 (anti-discrimination, anti-ridicule) and RA 10754 (financial benefits).

questions.text: An architect asks: 'Does RA 10754 contain ramp dimensions or corridor widths?' What is the correct answer, and where should the architect look for those specifications?

options.text: Yes — RA 10754 Section 32 contains all physical accessibility dimensions including ramp slopes and corridor widths
No — RA 10754 addresses benefits, VAT, and penalties only; physical dimensions are in BP 344 and the PD 1096 IRR
Yes — the 2016 RA 10754 IRR added an Appendix with metric dimensions for all accessible building elements
No — physical dimensions are solely in NCDA administrative orders, not in BP 344 or any statute

rationale.summary: RA 10754 contains no physical dimensions — it governs benefits, VAT, and penalties. Physical accessibility dimensions are in BP 344 and the PD 1096 IRR.
rationale.explanation: RA 10754 (2016) amends RA 7277 to expand financial benefits (20% discount, 12% VAT exemption) and strengthen penalties. It contains no millimeter-based specifications for ramps, corridors, parking, doors, or any other building element. Physical accessibility specifications are in BP 344 (the Accessibility Law) and its 2024 Revised IRR issued by DPWH, cross-referenced with PD 1096 (National Building Code) Rules VII and VIII. This law-dimension separation is a critical distinction tested on the LEA.
common_misconceptions: Searching RA 10754 for physical design standards when it only addresses benefits and penalties
Attributing dimensional requirements to NCDA instead of BP 344 and DPWH

questions.explanation: This question enforces the law-dimension separation principle — RA 10754 = benefits and penalties; BP 344 = physical specifications. A critical distinction for the LEA.

questions.text: Under RA 10524 amending RA 7277, what is the minimum percentage of positions in national government agencies that must be reserved for PWDs?

options.text: 2% of all positions in national government agencies and corporations
5% of all positions, consistent with the senior citizens employment quota
1% of all positions in national government agencies, offices, or corporations
10% of entry-level positions only, with no requirement for senior or technical roles

rationale.summary: RA 10524 requires at least 1% of all positions in national government agencies to be reserved for PWDs.
rationale.explanation: RA 10524 amends RA 7277 to require national government agencies, offices, and government-owned or controlled corporations to reserve at least 1% of all their positions for PWDs. For private companies with more than 100 employees, RA 10524 encourages (but does not strictly mandate under the same penalty structure) a similar 1% allocation through policy direction and tax incentives.
common_misconceptions: Stating 2% or 5% instead of 1% for the government employment quota
Confusing the 1% government quota with the private sector provision, which is encouraged rather than strictly mandated

questions.explanation: This question tests the 1% government employment quota under RA 10524 — a specific figure tested as a straightforward recall item on the LEA.

questions.text: A building owner installs a ramp that exceeds BP 344 minimum requirements in width and handrail specifications, going beyond what the code mandates. Under RA 7277, what additional tax benefit may be available for this discretionary expenditure?

options.text: A 25% additional deduction — the same as the PWD wage deduction — applied to all accessibility construction costs
A 50% additional deduction from taxable income on the direct costs of improvements that go beyond what BP 344 already requires
A full 100% tax credit on all accessibility improvements, regardless of whether they exceed BP 344 requirements
No additional benefit — tax incentives apply only to mandatory BP 344 compliance expenditures, not discretionary upgrades

rationale.summary: RA 7277 allows an additional 50% deduction on the direct costs of accessibility improvements that exceed what BP 344 already requires.
rationale.explanation: RA 7277 and its implementing regulations provide that when a building owner makes accessibility improvements beyond the minimum requirements of BP 344, an additional deduction equivalent to 50% of the direct costs of those discretionary improvements may be claimed from taxable income. This applies only to the excess — the portion that exceeds mandatory compliance. The mandatory BP 344-required work does not earn the 50% bonus deduction; only above-and-beyond improvements qualify.
common_misconceptions: Confusing the 50% accessibility deduction with the 25% PWD wage deduction
Applying the 50% deduction to all accessibility work rather than only the above-BP-344-minimum portion

questions.explanation: This question tests the 50% additional deduction for above-minimum accessibility improvements — and the critical condition that it applies only to expenditures beyond what BP 344 already mandates.

questions.text: A candidate is asked on the LEA: 'Which law should you cite for the minimum ramp clear width and maximum ramp slope?' What is the correct answer?

options.text: RA 7277 and RA 9442 — the Magna Carta laws that establish the right to accessible facilities including specific ramp dimensions
RA 10754 — the 2016 amendment that consolidated all physical accessibility specifications into one statute
BP 344 and its 2024 Revised IRR — the Accessibility Law and its implementing rules contain all physical dimension specifications
PD 1096 Rule VII — the National Building Code is the sole source for all accessible building dimensions

rationale.summary: Physical dimensions (ramp width, slope, handrails, etc.) come from BP 344 and its 2024 IRR — not from RA 7277/9442/10754, which address rights and benefits only.
rationale.explanation: BP 344 (the Accessibility Law) and its 2024 Revised IRR issued by DPWH contain all millimeter-based physical specifications: ramp widths, slopes, landing lengths, corridor widths, parking stall dimensions, fixture heights, etc. RA 7277, RA 9442, and RA 10754 establish rights, discounts, VAT exemptions, employment provisions, and penalties — none contain physical dimensions. PD 1096 (National Building Code) provides general building standards that coexist with BP 344. For accessibility-specific dimensions, BP 344 IRR is the primary citation.
common_misconceptions: Citing RA 7277 or RA 9442 for physical dimensions — these laws contain no millimeter specifications
Citing PD 1096 alone as the source for accessible ramp dimensions

questions.explanation: This law-separation question tests whether candidates correctly route physical specifications to BP 344 IRR — not to RA 7277/9442/10754, which govern rights and benefits.

questions.text: Under the Philippine PWD legal framework, a pharmacy refuses to honor a PWD's 20% discount and 12% VAT exemption. Under RA 10754, what additional consequences beyond the fine may apply for repeated refusals?

options.text: The pharmacy owner faces a civil damages lawsuit only — criminal liability does not apply to commercial discount refusals, which are treated as civil matters
The pharmacy faces up to ₱300,000 fine and up to 6 years imprisonment, plus possible suspension or revocation of business permits for serious or repeated offenses
The pharmacy loses its VAT registration only — no imprisonment is imposed for commercial discount violations, focusing on tax compliance
The pharmacy owner is referred to the BIR for tax audit only — pharmacy discount violations are treated as tax disputes, not criminal acts

rationale.summary: RA 10754 imposes up to ₱300,000 fine and up to 6 years imprisonment, plus possible business permit suspension or revocation for serious or repeated violations.
rationale.explanation: RA 10754 and RA 9442 establish a comprehensive penalty framework for violations of PWD privileges: fines up to ₱300,000; imprisonment up to 6 years; or both at the court's discretion. For serious or repeated offenses, administrative consequences include suspension or revocation of business permits/licenses. Refusal to honor PWD discounts is an explicit trigger for these penalties — it is not merely a civil dispute or a tax matter.
common_misconceptions: Assuming pharmacy discount refusals are civil-only matters without criminal exposure
Believing penalties are limited to fines without imprisonment for commercial violations

questions.explanation: This evaluation question tests the full scope of RA 10754 penalties — fine, imprisonment, AND business permit consequences — applied to a concrete commercial scenario.

questions.text: Under RA 9442 and RA 10754, what are the two main financial benefits a PWD receives on qualifying goods and services?

options.text: 15% discount and exemption from 10% VAT on specified goods and services, providing moderate financial relief.
20% discount and exemption from the 12% VAT on specified goods and services for the exclusive use of the PWD
25% discount and exemption from 12% VAT on all retail goods regardless of purpose, offering substantial savings across a wide range of purchases.
20% discount on medical services only; VAT exemption applies only to medicines and transportation, limiting the scope of financial benefits.

rationale.summary: PWDs are entitled to a 20% discount AND exemption from the 12% VAT on qualifying transactions for the PWD's exclusive use and enjoyment.
rationale.explanation: RA 7277 as amended by RA 9442 and RA 10754 grants PWDs: (1) a 20% discount on qualifying goods and services; (2) exemption from the 12% VAT on those same transactions. Both benefits apply together and are conditioned on the transaction being for the PWD's exclusive use and enjoyment — not for others. Qualifying categories include medicines, medical/dental services, transportation, hotel accommodation, restaurant meals, recreation, and burial services.
common_misconceptions: Stating 15% or 25% instead of 20% for the discount
Believing the VAT exemption applies independently of the discount or to different categories

questions.explanation: This question tests the two core financial benefits — 20% discount and 12% VAT exemption — as a pair, since both must be cited together for a complete answer.

questions.text: Which Philippine law is known as the 'Magna Carta for Persons with Disability,' and what year was it enacted?

options.text: RA 9442, enacted in 2007 — the law that expanded PWD privileges and added anti-discrimination provisions
RA 7277, enacted in 1992 — the foundational law establishing rights, privileges, and protections for PWDs
RA 10754, enacted in 2016 — the law that added the 12% VAT exemption and 20% discount for PWDs
BP 344, enacted in 1983 — the Accessibility Law mandating accessible building design for PWDs

rationale.summary: RA 7277 (1992) is the Magna Carta for Persons with Disability — the foundational law in the Philippine PWD rights framework.
rationale.explanation: RA 7277, enacted in 1992, is formally titled the 'Magna Carta for Persons with Disability.' It establishes the comprehensive framework for PWD rights including employment, education, health, rehabilitation, and accessibility. RA 9442 (2007) and RA 10754 (2016) are amendments that expand specific provisions of RA 7277. BP 344 (1983) predates RA 7277 and deals specifically with building accessibility — it is the technical implementation law, not the rights-granting charter.
common_misconceptions: Confusing RA 9442 with the Magna Carta — RA 9442 is an amendment, not the original charter
Associating BP 344 with the Magna Carta title — BP 344 is the Accessibility Law, not the Magna Carta

questions.explanation: This foundational recall question tests the correct law name and year for the Magna Carta — commonly confused with its amendments RA 9442 and RA 10754.

questions.text: Tracing the penalty evolution across the PWD law amendments, what is the current maximum criminal fine under the most recent law (RA 10754) for violations of PWD privileges and accessibility provisions?

options.text: ₱50,000 — the original BP 344 penalty, still in effect as the primary accessibility enforcement fine, despite subsequent amendments
₱100,000 — the RA 7277 Sec. 46 penalty, which superseded the original BP 344 fine, reflecting an increase in enforcement measures
₱200,000 — the RA 9442 amendment penalty, updated in 2007 to address inflation and increased enforcement needs
₱300,000 — the RA 10754 maximum, the current controlling standard with up to 6 years imprisonment

rationale.summary: The current maximum criminal fine is ₱300,000 under RA 10754, combined with up to 6 years imprisonment — the most recent amendment controls.
rationale.explanation: The penalty evolution: BP 344 original = ₱50,000 (no jail term); RA 7277 Sec. 46 = ₱100,000 + 6 months to 2 years; RA 9442 amendment = ₱200,000 + 6 months to 6 years; RA 10754 amendment = ₱300,000 + up to 6 years. The most recent law (RA 10754, 2016) controls. The ₱50,000 original BP 344 penalty is the most common distractor — it is frequently offered as an answer because candidates remember seeing it in BP 344, not realizing it has been superseded.
common_misconceptions: Citing the original ₱50,000 BP 344 fine as the current maximum
Stating ₱200,000 (RA 9442) instead of the higher ₱300,000 (RA 10754)

questions.explanation: This question tests the penalty progression across all four laws and requires candidates to select the highest (RA 10754) as the current controlling standard.
